predecessors.name: Norman England
predecessors.text: Normandy, which Geoffrey of Anjou took when 'in January 1144 he advanced into Rouen' (The Anarchy page)

predecessors.name: Angevins
predecessors.text: Anjou, Maine and Touraine, the lands of Geoffrey of Anjou (Cliopatria 'Angevins' row, 1126-1146)

predecessors.name: Kingdom of France
predecessors.text: Aquitaine, Gascony and Poitou brought by Eleanor's marriage to Henry in 1152, which Cliopatria draws as Kingdom of France in 1139-1151

successors.name: Kingdom of France
successors.text: Normandy, Anjou, Maine, Touraine and the other continental lands lost to Philip II in 1204-1206 (Poitou goes to the county of Poitou, Gascony to the duchy of Aquitaine)

successors.name: County of Poitou
successors.text: Poitou, conquered by Philip II in 1205

successors.name: Duchy of Aquitaine
successors.text: the Gascon core of Aquitaine (Gascony and the Gironde) that the duchy-of-aquitaine dossier draws from 1204

successors.name: Kingdom of England
successors.text: the 1206 shape without Gascony: England, the Welsh March and Ireland

rulers.name: Geoffrey Plantagenet (Geoffrey of Anjou)
rulers.title: Duke of Normandy and Count of Anjou

ledger.x: 1144: Geoffrey of Anjou takes Rouen and becomes duke of Normandy, the beginning of the Angevin dominion.
1147: Cliopatria joins Anjou, Maine and Touraine to Normandy.
1151: Louis VII recognises Henry as duke of Normandy and takes the Norman Vexin.
1152: Henry marries Eleanor and becomes duke of Aquitaine, land that Cliopatria draws as French until then.
1154: Henry buys back Vernon and Neuf-Marché from Louis VII.
25 October 1154: Stephen dies and Henry becomes King Henry II of England, joining England to the Angevin lands.
1157: the Scots hand back the north of England.
September 1158: Conan IV surrenders Nantes to Henry II.
1159: Henry takes Cahors and Quercy from Toulouse.
November 1160: Henry II seizes the Norman Vexin when his son marries Louis VII's daughter Margaret.
1164: Henry II seizes lands on the border between Brittany and Normandy.
1166: Henry II forces Conan IV to abdicate and takes the duchy under his guardianship.
1167: Henry marches into Auvergne.
17 October 1171: Henry II lands at Waterford and takes Dublin, Wexford and Waterford as crown land, with Leinster held of him by Strongbow.
1173: Raymond V of Toulouse pays homage to Henry at Limoges.
1174: William the Lion of Scotland becomes Henry's vassal by the Treaty of Falaise.
6 October 1175: the Treaty of Windsor makes Ruaidri Ua Conchobair Henry's vassal over the rest of Ireland.
February 1177: John de Courcy conquers east Ulster.
May 1177: Henry makes his son John Lord of Ireland and the Treaty of Windsor lapses in practice.
1177: the kingdoms of Thomond and Desmond are granted to Anglo-Normans.
1181: Henry's son Geoffrey becomes duke of Brittany and the guardianship ends.
1181: Brittany under Henry II's son Geoffrey is a protectorate of the empire.
1183: Raymond V of Toulouse retakes Cahors.
1185: Nantes returns to the Duchy of Brittany.
1188: Raymond V attacks again, joined by the Lusignans, ending his homage.
July 1189: Henry II gives up his claim to Auvergne to Philip II.
5 December 1189: Richard I annuls the Treaty of Falaise and Scotland is free again.
1193: Philip II takes Gisors and the Norman Vexin while Richard I is a captive.
By John's accession in 1199 Berry is lost.
May 1200: by the Treaty of Le Goulet John gives Philip II the county of Évreux.
1202: Philip II invades Normandy.
1204: Normandy falls to Philip II.
1204: the fighting for Normandy ends with Philip's conquest.
1204: Anjou is occupied by Philip II.
1204: Touraine is confiscated from John.
1204: Maine passes to Philip with Anjou and Touraine (bridging).
1204: the Gascon core of Aquitaine, John's only continental holding, becomes the duchy of Aquitaine's own.
1205: Poitou is conquered by Philip II.
1206: Brittany leaves the Angevin protectorate (begun in 1181 after the occupation of 1166-1181).
1206: the last continental lands north and east of Gascony are gone.
1209: the last year of Cliopatria's Angevin row; from 1210 the same land (England, Ireland, Gascony) is the Kingdom of England.

wars.name: Henry II's Toulouse campaign
wars.outcome: Henry gathered his army at Poitiers in June 1159, could not take Toulouse itself but took Cahors and the Garonne castles of Quercy; Raymond V 'finally gave up' and paid homage at Limoges in 1173, retook Cahors in 1183 and attacked again in 1188.

wars.name: Henry II's Welsh expeditions
wars.outcome: 'Henry attacked Wales three times, in 1157, 1158 and 1163', then 'undertook a fourth invasion in 1164, this time with a massive army'; the page says Wales 'obtained good terms provided it paid homage to the Plantagenets' and 'remained almost self-ruling'.

wars.name: Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland
wars.outcome: The barons landed at Bannow Bay on 1 May 1169, Dublin and Waterford fell in 1170, Henry II landed at Waterford on 17 October 1171 and took Dublin, Wexford and Waterford as crown land; the Treaty of Windsor (6 October 1175) split Ireland into two spheres; John…

wars.name: Revolt of 1173-1174 and the Scottish war
wars.outcome: William the Lion was captured at Alnwick (1174) and signed the Treaty of Falaise, placing English garrisons in Edinburgh, Roxburgh, Jedburgh and Berwick; Richard I annulled the treaty on 5 December 1189.

wars.name: Capetian-Angevin wars of Richard I's reign
wars.outcome: Philip II took Berry strongholds in 1188; Henry II renounced his claim to suzerainty over Auvergne in July 1189 (Philip II page; the Angevin Empire page has Richard recognising it as Philip's demesne without a year); Philip demanded the Vexin in January 1192…

wars.name: Philip II's conquest of Normandy and the Angevin lands
wars.outcome: Philip summoned John to Paris in 1202, declared him in breach of his feudal duties and invaded; Mirebeau (July 1202) captured the rebels; Chateau Gaillard fell in March 1204; by August Philip held Normandy, Anjou and Poitou; John took Angers in 1206 and a…

certainty.note: No treaty line or survey fixes the empire's frontiers on the pages opened: the English-Scottish border (Tweed), the Welsh March, the Irish pale and the frontiers with the French crown are approximate.
